To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Autistic individuals demonstrate intact sensorimotor learning but show greater spatial variability during motor execution.

the motor execution of autistic individuals was less accurate and more variable than non autistic individuals and that autistic individuals showed a reduction in spatial variability at peak velocities, but an increase in spatial variability at the peak acceleration, indicating specific differences in feedforward and feedback sensorimotor control during sensorimotor motor learning.

the motor learning in autism is characterized by: (i) a reduction in accuracy, but not in variability; (ii) intact feedforward based control, but impaired feedback based control; and (iii) intact early feedback based control, but disrupted later feedback based control.

the nature of the motor system, and how it develops, in individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD).

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found that whilst autistic individuals develop new motor representations (i.e., internal action models) during sensorimotor leaning, these representations are not executed as accurately as those of non autistic controls.
we have shown that autistic individuals can learn new motor tasks, but that they do not learn them in the same way as non-autistic people.
autistic individuals have intact sensorimotor control, but are less efficient at learning new motor actions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can see a difference in how autistic and non autistic individuals learn a new motor skill, but that this difference is not related to the ability to learn the new task.
we can use kinematic markers of movement to identify specific differences in the control processes that underpin the acquisition of new movements.

autistic individuals are able to learn new motor actions but they do this with less precision and with greater variability than non autistic individuals and that these differences are related to differences at the planning stage of motor control.
